sinus-infection.title: Sinus Infection Red Flags: When It's an Emergency | NPCWoods
sinus-infection.description: Eye swelling, vision changes, a stiff neck, confusion. Chris Woods, NP, lists the sinus infection signs that mean the ER, not a text visit.
sinus-infection.h1: Sinus infection red flags: when it's an emergency
sinus-infection.crumb: Red flags: when a sinus infection is an emergency
sinus-infection.og_alt: Sinus infection red flags: when it's an emergency. Chris Woods, NP. $59 text visits.
sinus-infection.lede: Most sinus infections are miserable and still harmless. Your sinuses sit next to your eyes and just in front of your brain, so a rare few spread. Keep this list handy. If you meet it, you do not text me first. You go.
thread: My face hurts and now my eyelid is puffy and red. Is that still sinus?
A puffy, red eyelid with fever, pain when you move the eye, or blurry vision is not a wait-and-see sinus. That is the ER today. Plain pressure behind the cheeks with a normal eye can be a text visit.
sinus-infection.er_text: Swelling, redness, or pain around one eye. Blurry or double vision. Pain when you move your eye, or an eye that bulges or will not move normally. A sudden, severe headache, the worst of your life. A stiff neck, confusion, or you are hard to wake. New swelling of the forehead. High fever with shaking chills, a racing heart, or you feel like you might pass out. Those are not text-visit problems.
sinus-infection.fig_title: Sinus infection red flags that mean go to the ER
fig_rows: Swelling or redness around one eye
Pain when you move the eye
sinus-infection.fig_alt: Red warning card titled Go to the ER or call 911, do not text first. Six sinus infection red flags: swelling or redness around one eye, blurry or double vision, pain when moving the eye, worst headache of your life, stiff neck or confusion, and forehead swelling with high fever.
sinus-infection.fig_caption: If you see any of these, skip the text. Go to the ER or call 911.

sections.h2: Why the eye and the brain matter
p: Your sinuses are hollow spaces in the bones of your face. The ones between your eyes and behind your forehead share thin walls with the eye socket, and they sit just in front of the brain.

In rare cases, infection pushes through those walls. Around the eye, that is called periorbital or orbital cellulitis. It can threaten your sight within a day or two, and it is more common in kids. Behind the forehead, infection can reach the bone or the lining of the brain.

These are rare. They are also the reason I take a puffy eyelid seriously. An emergency team can scan the area, start treatment through an IV, and bring in an eye or ENT surgeon the same day. I cannot do any of that from a phone.

ul: A fever of 102°F or higher that lasts more than 3 to 4 days.
Face pain or a headache that is severe and keeps climbing instead of easing.
New swelling of the cheek, upper gum, or roof of the mouth.
A weak immune system from cancer care, a transplant, or medicines that lower your immunity, plus a fever.
p_after: These are not 911 problems, but they are not wait-a-week problems either. Urgent care or your regular clinic today is the right door.

p: Some people have less room for error. If this is you, the red list counts double.
ul: Kids, because eye infections from the sinuses happen more often in children.
Diabetes, cancer care, a transplant, or medicines that lower your immunity.
Past sinus or face surgery, or a recent blow to the face.
Pregnancy with a fever.
p_after: For these groups I lower the bar for sending you in, and you should too. A same-day exam is a small price next to a rare, serious turn.

p: Most sinus trouble is a good fit for a text visit. Think stuffy nose, face pressure, thick drainage, and post-nasal drip, with clear eyes, a soft neck, and a clear head.
ul: Symptoms lasting 10 days or more without getting better.
You started to get better, then got worse again.
Pressure over the cheeks or forehead with a low fever or none.
No eye, vision, neck, or thinking changes at all.
p_after: I ask about the timeline, your temperature, your eyes, your neck, and any health conditions. If anything on the red list shows up, I tell you to go in. You do not pay for a $59 visit when I tell you text care is not safe.

p: I will not talk you out of the ER. Pressure behind the eyes is common. A swollen, red eye is not. A headache with congestion is common. The worst headache of your life, a stiff neck, or confusion is not.
When you are not sure, go. You can always text me afterward for follow-up once you are stable.

faq: Can a sinus infection spread to the eye?
Rarely, yes. Swelling and redness of the eyelid, pain when moving the eye, or blurry or double vision can mean infection around the eye. That needs the ER the same day.
Is a sinus headache ever an emergency?
Usual sinus pressure is not. A sudden, severe headache, a stiff neck, confusion, or a headache with a high fever that keeps climbing needs emergency care right away.
How long is too long for a sinus infection?
If symptoms last 10 days without improving, or you get better and then worse again, it is time to be checked. A text visit can fit if there are no red flags.
Should I text you if my eye is swelling?
No. Go to the ER or call 911 first. You can text later for follow-up once you are stable and back in a state I can treat.
sources: American Academy of Otolaryngology, ENT Health. Sinusitis.

ear-infection.title: Ear Infection Red Flags and When to Go In | NPCWoods
ear-infection.description: Swelling behind the ear, a drooping face, a stiff neck, sudden hearing loss. Chris Woods, NP, lists the ear infection signs that mean the ER.
ear-infection.h1: Ear infection red flags: when to go in
ear-infection.crumb: Red flags: when an ear infection needs the ER
ear-infection.og_alt: Ear infection red flags: when to go in. Chris Woods, NP. $59 text visits.
ear-infection.lede: Ear pain can be loud and still be simple. A few ear problems are not simple. The ear sits next to bone, a face nerve, and the brain. If you meet this list, you do not text me first. You go.
bubbles: Lump behind the ear? Go in
thread: My ear has hurt for three days and now the bone behind it is red and sore.
Redness, swelling, or a tender bump behind the ear, especially with fever, is a go-in-today problem, not a text. Plain ear pain with a normal face, neck, and balance can be a text visit.
ear-infection.er_text: Swelling, redness, or a tender lump behind the ear, or the ear pushed out from your head. One side of your face drooping or weak. A stiff neck, a severe headache, confusion, or you are very hard to wake. Sudden spinning dizziness with vomiting, or you cannot walk straight. High fever with shaking chills or a racing heart. If a face droop comes with arm weakness or slurred speech, call 911 right away: that can be a stroke. Those are not text-visit problems.
ear-infection.fig_title: Ear infection red flags that mean go to the ER
fig_rows: Swelling or a lump behind the ear
Ear pushed out from the head
ear-infection.fig_alt: Red warning card titled Go to the ER or call 911, do not text first. Six ear infection red flags: swelling or a lump behind the ear, ear pushed out from the head, face drooping on one side, stiff neck or severe headache, spinning dizziness and cannot walk straight, and high fever with confusion.
ear-infection.fig_caption: If you see any of these, skip the text. Go to the ER or call 911.

sections.h2: Why the bone behind the ear matters
p: Behind your ear is the mastoid, a honeycomb of bone that connects to the middle ear. Rarely, a middle ear infection spreads into it. That is mastoiditis. It shows up as redness, swelling, and tenderness behind the ear, often with fever and drainage, and the ear can stick out.

The nerve that moves your face also runs through the ear, so a bad infection can make one side of the face droop. The brain sits just above. These problems need imaging, treatment through an IV, and sometimes surgery. That is ER and ENT work, not a phone.

sections.h2: Sudden hearing loss is its own emergency
p: If hearing in one ear drops suddenly, over hours or a few days, get checked right away. Sudden hearing loss of the inner ear does best with early treatment, and waiting can make it permanent.
An ear that feels plugged during a cold is common. An ear that suddenly goes quiet, often with ringing or dizziness, is not. Tell the clinic the words sudden hearing loss.

ul: A fever of 102.2°F (39°C) or higher.
Pus or fluid draining from the ear along with severe pain.
Diabetes or a weak immune system with ear canal pain that keeps getting worse. That combination can spread into the skull bone.
A baby under 3 months with a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. Call your child's clinic right away.

p: Some people have less room for error. If this is you, the red list counts double.
ul: Babies and toddlers with fever, because they cannot tell you where it hurts.
Diabetes, especially in older adults with a painful, draining ear canal.
Cancer care, a transplant, or medicines that lower your immunity.
A cochlear implant, ear tubes, or recent ear surgery.
p_after: For these groups I lower the bar for sending you in, and you should too. A same-day exam beats a slow, quiet spread into bone.

p: Plenty of ear pain is a good fit for a text visit, especially in adults.
ul: Ear pain for a few days with a low fever or none.
Ear pain that started with a cold and is not better after 2 to 3 days.
Swimmer's ear: an itchy, sore ear canal with no spreading redness.
A normal face, neck, balance, and hearing that is only muffled.
p_after: I ask about fever, drainage, hearing, dizziness, and your face. If anything on the red list shows up, I send you in. You do not pay for a $59 visit when I tell you text care is not safe.

faq: Is swelling behind the ear an emergency?
Redness, swelling, or a tender lump behind the ear, especially with fever or an ear that sticks out, can mean the infection reached the bone. Get seen the same day, at the ER if you feel sick.
Can an ear infection make your face droop?
Rarely. The nerve that moves the face runs through the ear. Any new face droop needs emergency care, and with arm weakness or slurred speech, call 911 because it can be a stroke.
When is hearing loss an emergency?
Hearing that drops suddenly in one ear, over hours to a few days, should be checked right away. Early treatment gives the best chance of recovery.
Should I text you if I am dizzy and throwing up?
If the room is spinning, you are vomiting, or you cannot walk straight, go in first. You can text later for follow-up once you are stable.

skin-infection.title: Skin Infection Red Flags: Spreading Redness and Fever | NPCWoods
skin-infection.description: Redness racing past your pen line, pain worse than it looks, fever, dark or blistering skin. Chris Woods, NP, lists when a skin infection is an emergency.
skin-infection.h1: Skin infection red flags: when it's spreading
skin-infection.crumb: Red flags: when a skin infection is an emergency
skin-infection.og_alt: Skin infection red flags: when it's spreading. Chris Woods, NP. $59 text visits.
skin-infection.lede: Most skin infections stay put and heal. A few spread fast, go deep, or reach the blood. A pen line on your skin is the best tool you have. If the redness races past it, or you meet this list, you do not text me first. You go.
bubbles: Racing past the line? Go now
Pain way worse than it looks
thread: I drew a line around the red spot last night. This morning it's two inches past it and I have chills.
Fast spread plus chills is the ER today, not a text. A small red patch that stays inside the line, with no fever, can be a text visit.
skin-infection.er_text: Redness that races past your pen line within a few hours. Pain far worse than the skin looks. Skin turning purple, gray, or black, large blisters, or numb skin over the red area. Fever with shaking chills, a racing heart, fast breathing, clammy skin, or confusion. Redness and swelling around the eye, or swelling in the neck that makes it hard to swallow or breathe. Those are not text-visit problems.
skin-infection.fig_title: Skin infection red flags that mean go to the ER
fig_rows: Swelling near the eye or neck
skin-infection.fig_alt: Red warning card titled Go to the ER or call 911, do not text first. Six skin infection red flags: redness racing past the pen line, pain worse than it looks, dark, blistered, or numb skin, fever with chills or confusion, racing heart and fast breathing, and swelling near the eye or neck.
skin-infection.fig_caption: If you see any of these, skip the text. Go to the ER or call 911.

sections.h2: Why fast spread and bad pain matter
p: Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper layers of the skin. Most cases heal with care at home. Two rare turns change everything.

One is infection reaching the blood, which can turn into sepsis, the body's extreme reaction to an infection. Watch for confusion, shivering or feeling very cold, extreme pain, clammy skin, a racing heart, or shortness of breath.

The other is necrotizing fasciitis, a fast infection along the deeper tissue. Early signs are red, warm, swollen skin that spreads quickly, fever, and severe pain, including pain beyond the red area. Both need hospital care within hours. Neither is a text.
Take a pen and trace the edge of the redness. Write the time next to it and snap a photo. Check it every few hours.
A little growth over the first day can happen, even once care starts. Racing well past the line in a few hours is different. So are new red streaks running up an arm or leg from the sore spot.

ul: Red streaks running up the arm or leg from the sore spot.
A boil or bump that is large, very painful, or soft in the middle and may need draining.
Any bite on the hand, or a cat or human bite anywhere.
Diabetes, poor circulation, or a weak immune system with a foot or leg infection.
Redness that is not better after 2 days of care.

p: Some people have less room for error. If this is you, the red list counts double.
ul: Diabetes, especially with a sore or blister on the foot.
Poor circulation, long-term leg swelling, or lymphedema.
Cancer care, a transplant, liver or kidney disease, or medicines that lower your immunity.
A fresh surgery wound, a deep puncture, or an injury from salt or brackish water.
p_after: For these groups I lower the bar for sending you in, and you should too. Skin infections move faster when the body has less to fight with.

p: Many skin problems are a good fit for a text visit with a clear photo.
ul: A small, warm, red patch with a clear edge and no fever.
Pain that matches what you see.
Mild crusty sores, like impetigo, on a small area.
A bug bite that is itchy and pink but staying inside your pen line.
p_after: Send a photo with your pen line in it. I check the size, the edge, your temperature, and your health history. If anything on the red list shows up, I send you in. You do not pay for a $59 visit when I tell you text care is not safe.

faq: How fast is too fast for a skin infection to spread?
If redness moves well past your pen line in a few hours, or you get fever and chills, go in now. Slow growth over the first day can happen, but recheck the line every few hours.
What does it mean if the pain is worse than the skin looks?
Pain far out of proportion to a mild-looking red area, especially with fever, can be an early sign of a deep, fast infection. That is an ER problem the same day.
Are red streaks from a cut dangerous?
Red streaks spreading from a wound can mean the infection is moving through the lymph channels. Get seen in person today, and go to the ER if you have a fever.
Should I text you if I have a fever and the redness is spreading?
No. Go to the ER first. You can text later for follow-up once you are stable and back in a state I can treat.
sources: American Academy of Dermatology. Cellulitis: Signs and symptoms.
